source_title: Stephen Fry Explains Why the V for Vendetta 20th Anniversary Comes ‘with a Mixture of Pride and Shame’ (Exclusive) - People.com
source_excerpt:
Fry tells PEOPLE it’s a “deep pleasure” to be associated with the film
Stephen Fry calls filming V for Vendetta with John Hurt an unforgettable highlight of the dystopian thriller
Fry says the film’s warnings feel especially relevant more than 20 years later
The movie returns to theaters for two anniversary screenings on Nov. 1 and Nov. 5
Stephen Fry says filming V for Vendetta over 20 years ago was “a treat from start to finish.”
The 69-year-old actor, who played Gordon Deitrich in the dystopian thriller, is reflecting on shooting the 2006 film ahead of its limited, two-night-only re-release in theaters.
“I came in knowing one thing — that I was going to have scenes with John Hurt, whom I had met and knew a little but had never worked with, and that this alone would be an unforgettable treat. As indeed it was,” Fry tells PEOPLE.
The James McTeigue-directed film was based on the 1988–89 DC Vertigo Comics limited series graphic novel of the same name. However, Fry admits he hadn’t read Alan Moore’s work beforehand, and was “sent a copy before traveling to Germany for the shoot.” The actor says he “read it in one breathless sitting, absolutely stunned by its quality.”
“I have since read as much Alan Moore as I could lay my hands on,” Fry shares. “ V for Vendetta ’s fear of a new rise in fascism? Is that timely these years later?! You hardly need ask.”
In addition to Fry and Hurt, the movie starred Natalie Portman, Hugo Weaving and Stephen Rea.
Fry says, “One of the deep pleasures of being associated with this picture is the number of times people have come to me and praised its acute relevance.”
“It’s an anniversary now that one meets with a mixture of pride and shame. Pride in how well the film was put together by James McTeigue and the Wachowskis and shame in how little our society has done to prevent its prophetic nature from being disproved,” Fry tells PEOPLE.
The moment from filming that still stands out to Fry was when they traveled to London to film the climactic final scene in which freedom fighters blow up the Houses of Parliament.
Fry still marvels at the fact they “managed to get permission for tanks and huge crowds to assemble in Whitehall, the very seat of government,” saying he assumed they’d “shoot in some huge green screen space in Pinewood or a not-very-convincing simulacrum of Westminster, but not that we’d be allowed in the heart of it.”
While he notes that things worked out “less than wonderfully” for his character, he says the fact that they “found time” for Gordon’s “small arc is wonderful.”
Still, reflecting on the movie, Fry shares that “it’s hard not to look at the bully boys that work for John Hurt’s totalitarian regime” and not see parallels to today.
Fry says films like V for Vendetta show the “importance of a cinema that can warn but still entertain while warning.”
Tickets fo r V for Vendetta ’s 20th anniversary screenings are available now online and at participating theater box offices. Showings are scheduled for Nov. 1 and Nov. 5. For more information, please visit FathomEntertainment.com .
